claim: Optical control of neural ensemble activity is crucial for understanding brain function and disease.
source: Optical control of neural ensemble activity is crucial for understanding brain function and disease, yet no technology can achieve optogenetic control of very large numbers of neurons at an extremely fast rate over a large volume.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of optical control in neuroscience research, representing established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: No existing technology can achieve optogenetic control of very large numbers of neurons at an extremely fast rate over a large volume.
source: Optical control of neural ensemble activity is crucial for understanding brain function and disease, yet no technology can achieve optogenetic control of very large numbers of neurons at an extremely fast rate over a large volume.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in existing technology, based on the authors' assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: State-of-the-art multiphoton holographic optogenetics requires high-power illumination that only addresses relatively small populations of neurons in parallel.
source: State-of-the-art multiphoton holographic optogenetics requires high-power illumination that only addresses relatively small populations of neurons in parallel.
evidence: This is a characterization of existing multiphoton holographic optogenetics technology based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: One-photon holographic techniques can stimulate more neurons with two to three orders lower power than multiphoton techniques, but with limited resolution or addressable volume.
source: Conversely, one-photon holographic techniques can stimulate more neurons with two to three orders lower power, but with limited resolution or addressable volume.
evidence: This claim compares one-photon and multiphoton techniques based on established knowledge of their characteristics.

claim: Two-photon holographic optogenetic systems are extremely expensive and sophisticated, which has precluded their broader adoption in the neuroscience community.
source: Perhaps most problematically, two-photon holographic optogenetic systems are extremely expensive and sophisticated which has precluded their broader adoption in the neuroscience community.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the field and the barriers to adoption of two-photon systems.

claim: 3D-MAP is a new one-photon light sculpting technique that modulates light dynamically in both the spatial and angular domain at multi-kHz rates.
source: To address this technical gap, we introduce a new one-photon light sculpting technique, three-dimensional multi-site random access photostimulation (3D-MAP), that overcomes these limitations by modulating light dynamically, both in the spatial and in the angular domain at multi-kHz rates.
evidence: This is a description of the novel technique introduced in this manuscript.

claim: 3D-MAP enables simultaneous photostimulation and imaging of dozens of user-selected neurons in the intact mouse brain in vivo with high spatio-temporal resolution.
source: We use 3D-MAP to interrogate neural circuits in 3D and demonstrate simultaneous photostimulation and imaging of dozens of user-selected neurons in the intact mouse brain in vivo with high spatio-temporal resolution.
evidence: This claim summarizes experimental results demonstrated in the manuscript.

claim: 3D-MAP can be broadly adopted for high-throughput all-optical interrogation of brain circuits owing to its powerful combination of scale, speed, simplicity, and cost.
source: 3D-MAP can be broadly adopted for high-throughput all-optical interrogation of brain circuits owing to its powerful combination of scale, speed, simplicity, and cost.
evidence: This is a forward-looking claim about the potential adoption of the technique based on its demonstrated characteristics.

claim: Optogenetics enables rapid and reversible control of neural activity.
source: Optogenetics enables rapid and reversible control of neural activity (Deisseroth, 2011; Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing optogenetics.

claim: Two-photon photostimulation has the advantages of high spatial resolution for precise neural activity control and relative immunity to tissue light scattering.
source: Two-photon photostimulation has the advantages of high spatial resolution for precise neural activity control and relative immunity to tissue light scattering, enabling stimulation of deep brain circuits.
evidence: This claim describes established advantages of two-photon photostimulation based on knowledge in the field.

claim: Two-photon holographic optogenetic photostimulation can only stimulate relatively small ensembles of neurons at a time, limited by the very high-power pulsed illumination required to achieve non-linear multiphoton absorption.
source: However, two-photon holographic optogenetic photostimulation can only stimulate relatively small ensembles of neurons at a time, limited by the very high-power pulsed illumination required to achieve non-linear multiphoton absorption.
evidence: This claim describes a limitation of two-photon holographic optogenetics based on established knowledge.

claim: High photon density heats brain tissue and can disturb brain activity and cause thermal damage.
source: High photon density heats brain tissue, and can disturb brain activity and cause thermal damage (Mardinly et al., 2018; Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on the effects of high photon density.

claim: The accessible volume for holographic two-photon photostimulation is limited by the coherence length of the laser being used.
source: The accessible volume for holographic two-photon photostimulation is also limited by the coherence length of laser being used, since holographic diffraction of femtosecond pulses to a large angle introduces severe pulse dispersion ('chirp'), substantially reducing pulse peak power (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work on pulse dispersion in holographic two-photon photostimulation.

claim: Multiphoton optogenetics has only been adopted by a small handful of groups, typically with much prior optical expertise, despite more than a decade since their introduction.
source: Thus, despite more than a decade since their introduction, multiphoton optogenetics has only been adopted by a small handful of groups, typically with much prior optical expertise.
evidence: This is an observational claim about the adoption of multiphoton optogenetics in the field.

claim: One-photon photostimulation systems require two to three orders of magnitude less laser power to activate neurons compared to two-photon systems.
source: In contrast, one-photon photostimulation systems require two to three orders of magnitude less laser power to activate neurons.
evidence: This claim compares power requirements between one-photon and two-photon systems based on established knowledge.

claim: One-photon photostimulation systems are much simpler to implement with far less expensive hardware than two-photon systems.
source: They are much simpler to implement with far less expensive hardware, and they can still achieve high-resolution photostimulation under limited light scattering conditions.
evidence: This claim compares the complexity and cost of one-photon versus two-photon systems based on knowledge of the technologies.

claim: Scanning-based one-photon photostimulation stimulates neurons sequentially by rapidly scanning a single focus across small neural clusters.
source: The first approach, scanning-based one-photon photostimulation, stimulates neurons sequentially by rapidly scanning a single focus across small neural clusters with scanning mirrors (Petreanu et al., 2009) or acousto-optic deflectors (AODs) (Losavio et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim describes an existing approach to one-photon photostimulation, supported by citations.

claim: Scanning-based one-photon photostimulation cannot photostimulate distributed ensembles simultaneously.
source: This method cannot photostimulate distributed ensembles simultaneously.
evidence: This is a limitation of scanning-based approaches based on their sequential nature.

claim: DMD-based widefield illumination has a large field-of-view and moderate lateral resolution but only modulates light in 2D.
source: This widefield illumination scheme has a large field-of-view (FOV) and moderate lateral resolution but only modulates light in 2D.
evidence: This describes characteristics of DMD-based widefield illumination based on knowledge of the technology.

claim: DMD-based widefield illumination has no axial sectioning ability and unwanted photostimulation may occur both above and below the focal plane.
source: There is no axial sectioning ability and unwanted photostimulation may occur both above and below the focal plane.
evidence: This describes a limitation of 2D widefield illumination based on knowledge of the technology.

claim: One-photon CGH generates 3D distributed foci by phase modulation of coherent light in Fourier space using a spatial light modulator.
source: The third approach, computer generated holography (CGH), generates 3D distributed foci by phase modulation of coherent light in Fourier space using a spatial light modulator (SLM) (Lutz et al., 2008; Anselmi et al., 2011; Szabo et al., 2014; Reutsky-Gefen et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the CGH approach with citations to prior work.

claim: The throughput of CGH is fundamentally limited by the number of degrees-of-freedom, which is determined by the number of pixels and the bit depth of the SLM.
source: First, the throughput of CGH that determines the number of accessible voxels is fundamentally limited by the number of degrees-of-freedom (DoF), which is determined by the number of pixels and the bit depth of the SLM, regardless of magnification and numerical aperture.
evidence: This describes a fundamental limitation of CGH based on the physics of the approach.

claim: The refresh rate of SLMs (tens to hundreds Hz) limits the speed of CGH.
source: Second, the refresh rate (tens to hundreds Hz) of SLMs limits the speed of CGH.
evidence: This describes a limitation of CGH based on the hardware characteristics of SLMs.

claim: CGH requires computing a 2D phase mask at the Fourier plane for a 3D hologram pattern, which is an ill-posed problem that requires iterative optimization with computation time on the order of minutes.
source: Third, CGH requires computing a 2D phase mask at the Fourier plane for a 3D hologram pattern, which is an ill-posed problem that requires iterative optimization, with computation time on the order of minutes (Zhang et al., 2017; Gerchberg, 1972; Leseberg, 1992; Xue et al., 2019) when shaping light across multiple z-planes.
evidence: This describes a computational limitation of CGH, supported by citations.

claim: One-photon CGH holograms composed of many illumination spots will suffer spatial cross-talk as out-of-focus light from each focused spot interacts, accidentally stimulating non-targeted neurons.
source: The fourth drawback of one-photon CGH is that holograms composed of many illumination spots will suffer spatial cross-talk as out-of-focus light from each focused spot interacts, accidentally stimulating non-targeted neurons.
evidence: This describes a limitation of one-photon CGH based on the physics of holographic illumination.

claim: The total number of degrees of freedom in 3D-MAP is determined by the product of the number of angles of the scanning mirror and the number of pixels of the DMD.
source: The total number of DoF is hence determined by the product of the number of angles of the scanning mirror and the number of pixels of the DMD (as opposed to the sum), resulting in a much larger DoF than existing one-photon optogenetic stimulation techniques (Lutz et al., 2008; Anselmi et al., 2011; Szabo et al., 2014; Reutsky-Gefen et al., 2013; Dhawale et al., 2010; Leifer et al., 2011; Adam et al., 2019; Werley et al., 2017; Sakai et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes a key advantage of 3D-MAP in terms of degrees of freedom, with citations to prior techniques.

claim: 3D-MAP achieves both high spatial resolution and a large accessible volume.
source: Thus, 3D-MAP achieves both high spatial resolution and a large accessible volume.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the capabilities of 3D-MAP based on its design principles.

claim: 3D-MAP is able to reduce spatial cross-talk by prioritizing illumination angles that minimize the stimulation of non-targeted areas.
source: Compared to one-photon CGH, 3D-MAP is able to reduce spatial cross-talk by prioritizing illumination angles that minimize the stimulation of non-targeted areas due to its high DoF.
evidence: This describes an advantage of 3D-MAP over CGH based on its design.

claim: 3D-MAP can pattern the entire addressable volume at multi-kHz rate, which exceeds the bandwidth of most neural circuits and is one order of magnitude faster than 3D CGH.
source: Thanks to the use of a DMD instead of an SLM, we can pattern the entire addressable volume at multi-kHz rate (the volumetric pattern refresh rate), which exceeds the bandwidth of most neural circuits and is one order of magnitude faster than 3D CGH.
evidence: This describes a speed advantage of 3D-MAP based on the use of a DMD.

claim: In 3D-MAP, the DMD and scanning mirrors are placed at conjugate image planes and time-synchronized.
source: Both devices are placed at conjugate image planes and time-synchronized (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes a key aspect of the 3D-MAP setup.

claim: To create a focused spot at an off-focus plane in 3D-MAP, a small aperture on the DMD rotates in a circle as the scanning mirrors sweep through a cone of projection angles.
source: To create a focused spot at an off-focus plane, a small aperture on the DMD rotates in a circle as the scanning mirrors sweep through a cone of projection angles (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the mechanism for creating off-focus spots in 3D-MAP, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: In 3D-MAP, the amount of light on any given target is quadratically proportional to the radius of the aperture.
source: The amount of light on any given target is quadratically proportional to the radius of the aperture.
evidence: This describes a relationship between aperture size and light intensity in 3D-MAP.

claim: In 3D-MAP experiments, 10 illumination angles are used for each 3D target.
source: In all our experiments, we use 10 illumination angles for each 3D target; additional illumination angles only introduce minor improvements (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This describes an experimental parameter choice, with data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: The maximum refresh rate of the DMD is 13 kHz, and each 3D volumetric pattern is generated by 10 masks on the DMD, so the maximum volumetric pattern rate is 1.3 kHz.
source: The maximum refresh rate of the DMD is 13 kHz, and each 3D volumetric pattern is generated by 10 masks on the DMD, so the maximum volumetric pattern rate is 1.3 kHz, which is more than an order of magnitude faster than conventional CGH with commercial SLMs.
evidence: This describes the speed capabilities of 3D-MAP based on hardware specifications.

claim: The DMD masks for 3D-MAP are based on ray tracing and can be calculated much faster than phase holograms in CGH.
source: In addition, the DMD masks for 3D-MAP are based on ray tracing and can be calculated much faster than phase holograms in CGH (Zhang et al., 2017; Gerchberg, 1972; Leseberg, 1992; Xue et al., 2019), enabling real-time or closed-loop applications such as mapping neural circuits (see below).
evidence: This describes a computational advantage of 3D-MAP, with citations to CGH computation methods.

claim: The 3D optical PSF of 3D-MAP indicates a spatial resolution of 5 × 5 × 18 μm³ with a 473 nm excitation wavelength.
source: The full-width-half-maximums (FWHMs) of the resulting 3D optical PSF indicate a spatial resolution of 5 × 5 × 18 μm3 with a 473 nm excitation wavelength.
evidence: This is a measurement of the optical resolution of 3D-MAP.

claim: 3D-MAP can simultaneously generate 25 foci at custom (x, y, z) locations in a 744 × 744 × 400 μm³ volume.
source: We also demonstrated the ability to simultaneously generate 25 foci at custom (x, y, z) locations in a 744 × 744 × 400 μm3 volume (Figure 2D).
evidence: This demonstrates the multi-site capability of 3D-MAP, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The foci on the edge of the accessible volume are slightly larger than the foci in the center generated by the same size aperture (63% larger along the x-axis and 38% larger along the z-axis on average for foci that are 300 µm away from the center).
source: The foci on the edge of the accessible volume are slightly larger than the foci in the center generated by the same size aperture (63% larger along the x-axis and 38% larger along the z-axis on average for foci that are 300 µm away from the center, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-J).
evidence: This describes a spatial variation in resolution across the field of view, with data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-J.

claim: Without the brain slice, the size of the focus was 11.7 × 11.7 × 42 μm³ (473 nm blue) and 10.4 × 10.4 × 50.7 μm³ (635 nm red).
source: Without the brain slice, the size of the focus was 11.7 × 11.7 × 42 μm3 (473 nm blue) and 10.4 × 10.4 × 50.7 μm3 (635 nm red).
evidence: This is a measurement of focus size without scattering.

claim: When generating the focus through 50, 100, and 150 μm thick brain slices, the size of the focus spot with blue light increased by 8%, 75%, and 269%, and the size of the focus spot with red light increased by 67%, 107%, and 114%, respectively.
source: When generating the focus through 50, 100, and 150 μm thick brain slices, the size of the focus spot with blue light increased by 8%, 75%, and 269%, and the size of the focus spot with red light increased by 67%, 107%, and 114%, respectively (averaged values measured along the x-axis and the z-axis).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of tissue scattering on focus size for different wavelengths and tissue thicknesses.

claim: The PPSF measurements show that 3D-MAP provides high-resolution photostimulation in vitro (lateral FWHM, 29 ± 0.8 μm; axial FWHM, 44 ± 1.6 μm, 9 cells).
source: The PPSF measurements show that 3D-MAP provides high-resolution photostimulation in vitro (lateral FWHM, 29 ± 0.8 μm; axial FWHM, 44 ± 1.6 μm, 9 cells, Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is a measurement of physiological spatial resolution in brain slices, shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: The spatial specificity of 3D-MAP is only approximately two-fold worse when compared to previous results using multiphoton optogenetics in comparable conditions.
source: Under these conditions, we found that the spatial specificity of 3D-MAP is only approximately two-fold worse when compared to our previous results using multiphoton optogenetics in comparable conditions (Pégard et al., 2017; Mardinly et al., 2018).
evidence: This compares the spatial specificity of 3D-MAP to prior multiphoton work, with citations.

claim: 3D-MAP evoked spiking resolution in brain slices is 16 ± 2.4 μm laterally and 44 ± 8.9 μm axially (n = 5 neurons).
source: Experimental results show that 3D-MAP enables high spatial specificity under all these conditions (Figure 3E–G shows in vitro results [5 cells], with lateral FWHM, 16 ± 2.4 μm; and axial FWHM, 44 ± 8.9 μm.
evidence: This is a measurement of spiking resolution in brain slices, shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: 3D-MAP evoked spiking resolution measured in vivo is 19 ± 3.7 μm laterally and 45 ± 6.1 μm axially (n = 8 neurons).
source: Figure 3H–J shows in vivo results (8 cells), with lateral FWHM, 19 ± 3.7 μm; and axial FWHM, 45 ± 6.1 μm).
evidence: This is a measurement of spiking resolution in vivo, shown in Figure 3H-J.

claim: 3D-MAP operates at low stimulation powers far below photodamage thresholds.
source: In addition to high spatio-temporal resolution and fast computational speed, 3D-MAP operates at low stimulation powers far below photodamage thresholds and is hence easily scalable to address large neural ensembles in distributed volumes of brain tissue.
evidence: This describes a safety advantage of 3D-MAP based on its low power requirements.

claim: Most connectivity maps exhibited spatial clusters when mapping synaptic input in space with 3D-MAP.
source: We generated excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) by sequential photostimulation of the entire volume and observed that most connectivity maps exhibited spatial clusters (Figure 4D–E) as typically observed when mapping synaptic input in space (Naka et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an observation from connectivity mapping experiments, with a citation to prior work showing similar results.

claim: The size of each cluster in connectivity maps is about 30 µm, which reaches the limit of spatial resolution measured in Figure 3A–B.
source: The size of each cluster is about 30 µm, which reaches the limit of spatial resolution measured in Figure 3A–B.
evidence: This relates the observed cluster size to the measured spatial resolution.

claim: Multi-site stimulation generates greater net input compared to the linear sum of individual responses by single stimulation (p = 0.0488 for 2–5 sites stimulation, two-way ANOVA).
source: We compared the photocurrents measured by multi-site simultaneous stimulation to the linear sum of individual responses by single stimulation (Figure 5D) and observed the multi-site stimulation generates greater net input (Figure 5E, p = 0.0488 for 2–5 sites stimulation, two-way analysis of variance [ANOVA)].
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of multi-site versus single-site stimulation responses, shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Multi-site simultaneous stimulation engages the activity of spatially distributed ensembles of neurons, which may facilitate polysynaptic network activity and engages network level properties of the circuit.
source: First, multi-site stimulation engages the activity of spatially distributed ensembles of neurons (rather than single neurons or small local clusters), which may facilitate polysynaptic network activity and engages network level properties of the circuit.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the advantages of multi-site stimulation.

claim: The co-expression level of stCoChR-p2A-H2B-GFP and jRCaMP1a is about 50% (sample size: 114 neurons expressing CoChR, 99 neurons expressing RcaMP1a, 54 neurons expressing both).
source: The co-expression level is about 50% (sample size: 114 neurons expressing CoChR, 99 neurons expressing RcaMP1a, 54 neurons expressing both).
evidence: This is a measurement of co-expression levels in the all-optical experiments.

claim: TTX completely blocked the light-induced calcium transients, demonstrating that they are due to calcium influx following light-evoked spiking.
source: Importantly, TTX completely blocked the light-induced calcium transients demonstrating that they are due to calcium influx following light-evoked spiking.
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating that observed calcium signals are due to neural activity.

claim: All-optical PPSF measurements across 10 neurons indicate a lateral resolution of 49 ± 21 µm and an axial resolution of 53 ± 28 µm.
source: Averaged measurements of all-optical PPSF across 10 neurons indicate a lateral resolution of 49 ± 21 µm and an axial resolution of 53 ± 28 µm (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a measurement of all-optical spatial resolution in vivo, shown in Figure 7E.

claim: 3D-MAP photostimulated and imaged 80 user-selected L2/3 neurons in vivo simultaneously with a total power of 480 µW out of the objective lens.
source: We photostimulated and imaged 80 user-selected L2/3 neurons in vivo simultaneously with a total power of 480 µW out of the objective lens (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This demonstrates high-throughput all-optical interrogation, shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: The average separation between neurons in the 80-neuron experiment is about 49 ± 26 µm.
source: The stimulation pattern is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and the average separation between neurons is about 49 ± 26 µm (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a measurement of neuron spacing in the experiment, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Neurons exhibit strong calcium activity primarily when they are stimulated, and minimal calcium activity when the adjacent neurons are stimulated.
source: We observe that neurons exhibit strong calcium activity primarily when they are stimulated, and minimal calcium activity when the adjacent neurons are stimulated.
evidence: This is an observation from the ensemble stimulation experiments demonstrating specificity.

claim: Under relatively sparse opsin expression conditions, 3D-MAP can be used to photo-activate user-defined spatially intermixed ensembles in the superficial layers of the mouse brain.
source: Thus, under relatively sparse opsin expression conditions, 3D-MAP can be used to photo-activate user-defined spatially intermixed ensembles in the superficial layers of the mouse brain.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the capabilities of 3D-MAP based on the experimental results.

claim: 3D-MAP is the first system to achieve 3D multi-site illumination with previously unattainable DoF by simultaneously sculpting the light field in both intensity and angular domains.
source: 3D-MAP is the first system to achieve 3D multi-site illumination with previously unattainable DoF by simultaneously sculpting the light field in both intensity and angular domains.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of 3D-MAP compared to prior work.

claim: One can build a 3D-MAP system for a small fraction of the cost of two-photon holographic optogenetic systems.
source: Perhaps most importantly for the broader neuroscience community, one can build a 3D-MAP system for a small fraction of the cost of two-photon holographic optogenetic systems (see Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a claim about the cost advantage of 3D-MAP, with reference to a cost comparison table.

claim: 3D-MAP is the first demonstration that uses 4D light field patterning for in vivo optogenetic photostimulation.
source: 3D-MAP is the first demonstration that uses 4D light field patterning for in vivo optogenetic photostimulation.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of 3D-MAP in the context of in vivo optogenetics.

claim: 3D-MAP achieves orders of magnitude more DoF than previous systems without extra hardware.
source: Hence, 3D-MAP achieves orders of magnitude more DoF without extra hardware.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantage of 3D-MAP in terms of degrees of freedom.

claim: The maximum defocus range of 3D-MAP is 720 µm whereas the MLA-based method only achieves 40 µm range in microscopy applications.
source: Therefore, the maximum defocus range of 3D-MAP is 720 µm (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) whereas the MLA-based method only achieves 40 µm range in microscopy applications.
evidence: This compares the axial range of 3D-MAP to a microlens array-based approach, with data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both one-photon and two-photon multi-site photostimulation are subject to spatial cross-talk, as out-of-focus light from one target may accidentally stimulate neurons that are at other focal planes.
source: Both one-photon and two-photon multi-site photostimulation are subject to spatial cross-talk, as out-of-focus light from one target may accidentally stimulate neurons that are at other focal planes, especially when the density of foci is high or when out-of-focus neurons are more photosensitive than the desired targets.
evidence: This describes a general limitation of multi-site photostimulation approaches.

claim: The cross-talk in the all-optical experiments is minimal under conditions of relatively sparse opsin expression as obtained with conventional in utero electroporation.
source: In Figure 7, we demonstrated that the cross-talk in our experiment is minimal under conditions of relatively sparse opsin expression as obtained with conventional in utero electroporation (Adesnik and Scanziani, 2010).
evidence: This is a claim about the minimal cross-talk observed in the experiments, with a citation to the expression method.

claim: When the separation between two adjacent neurons is closer than the all-optical PPSF, off-target effects are likely, even under sparse expression conditions.
source: However, when the separation between two adjacent neurons is closer than the all-optical PPSF, off-target effects are likely, even under sparse expression conditions.
evidence: This describes a limitation of 3D-MAP when neurons are too close together.

claim: 3D-MAP could potentially leverage its multi-kHz patterning speed to exploit the temporal domain by multiplexing patterns and targeting smaller subsets of neurons at a time in order to increase pattern sparsity.
source: Therefore, in addition to expression sparsity, we can also control the stimulation pattern's sparsity to mitigate spatial cross-talk. When the desired density of foci is high and cross-talk is expected, 3D-MAP could potentially leverage its multi-kHz patterning speed to exploit the temporal domain by multiplexing patterns and targeting smaller subsets of neurons at a time in order to increase pattern sparsity.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about a potential strategy to reduce cross-talk.

claim: Two-photon photostimulation techniques typically restrict the instantaneous power under the objective below 4 W to avoid photodamage.
source: For example, two-photon photostimulation techniques typically restrict the instantaneous power under the objective below 4 W to avoid photodamage (Sridharan, 2021; Mardinly et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes a power limitation of two-photon techniques, with citations.

claim: At full power, two-photon photostimulation techniques can simultaneously activate tens to over a hundred neurons.
source: At full power, two-photon photostimulation techniques can simultaneously activate tens to over a hundred neurons (Sridharan, 2021; Marshel et al., 2019; Mardinly et al., 2018; Dalgleish et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the capacity of two-photon techniques, with citations.

claim: 3D-MAP is able to photostimulate dozens of neurons simultaneously with only 480 µW out of the objective.
source: In contrast, 3D-MAP is able to photostimulate dozens of neurons simultaneously with only 480 µW out of the objective (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This compares the power requirements of 3D-MAP to two-photon techniques, with data in Figure 7F-G.

claim: The effective resolution of 3D-MAP in brain tissue is limited by scattering.
source: Like any other one-photon photostimulation technique, the effective resolution of 3D-MAP in brain tissue is limited by scattering.
evidence: This describes a fundamental limitation of one-photon techniques including 3D-MAP.

claim: Illumination with red shifted sources can reduce Rayleigh scattering and mitigate resolution loss through brain tissue.
source: As we show in Figures 2 and 6, illumination with red shifted sources can reduce Rayleigh scattering and mitigate resolution loss through brain tissue, but the accessible depth remains fundamentally limited to the first few hundreds of microns below the surface of the mouse brain and the scattering effect is more severe the deeper the stimulation is.
evidence: This describes a strategy to reduce scattering effects, with reference to data in Figures 2 and 6.

claim: To photostimulate neurons deeper inside the mammalian brain with 3D-MAP, the cortex can be surgically removed or implemented with a miniaturized microscope.
source: To photostimulate neurons deeper inside the mammalian brain with 3D-MAP, the cortex can be surgically removed (Adam et al., 2019; Dombeck et al., 2010; Marshel et al., 2012) or implemented with a miniaturized microscope (Szabo et al., 2014; Stamatakis et al., 2018) as it is routinely performed to image deep structures such as the hippocampus or the thalamus.
evidence: This describes potential strategies for accessing deeper brain regions, with citations to prior work.
